role: FPGA Engineer (signal processing lab of a research institute, probation complete)
headline: An electronic information engineering degree in Chengdu, then a job at a communications equipment research institute in the western high-tech zone, writing Vivado projects in the signal processing lab and staying late over one timing violation until the guard comes to lock up the lab building: an FPGA engineer
unit: The signal processing lab of a research institute in Chengdu's western high-tech zone that builds private-network communications and satellite ground-station equipment
education: Bachelor's degree in electronic information engineering
level: You write Verilog fluently, have built state machines, FIFOs and AXI interfaces, and can read waveforms in ModelSim. But on the board, things don't match the simulation; your mentor still has to fix the timing constraints on high-speed interfaces line by line, and in joint debugging with the hardware lab you often can't follow what they're saying.
intro: You studied electronic information engineering in Chengdu, and in your final year got an offer from this research institute in the western high-tech zone. You joined the signal processing lab to write FPGA designs under a mentor with twenty years in. The equipment you build goes into satellite ground stations and private-network base stations; signals coming down from the sky pass through a few thousand lines of your code first. Your probation is over, and from today on, part of what runs inside the chip on that board carries your name.
salary_note: Estimate: communications research institutes in Chengdu pay engineers a little over twenty percent below the national average, but contribute generously to the housing fund and occupational annuity, with a canteen, subsidized talent apartments, and project bonuses when a program milestone is passed. Raises follow professional titles, earned one rank at a time.

facts.label: Assistant Engineer (current level)
facts.value: 0-4 years, ¥8,300–10,500 a month (at this employer, estimated)

facts.label: What AI can't take
facts.value: Joint debugging with the hardware, software and systems teams

facts.label: Where AI is moving in
facts.value: Writing design documents, test reports and interface specs

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 36 related listings nationwide, 2 in this city (mostly campus hiring and internships)

day: Metro Line 2 to the western zone, then a shared bike from the station. The guard at the institute gate knows you and nods. You lock your phone in the phone cabinet at the lab building entrance and hang the key around your neck.
You open Vivado and pick up last night's synthesis results: one path in the timing report is negative by 0.3 nanoseconds, a multiplier in the FFT module you wrote.

Your mentor comes over, takes a look, and says you're two pipeline stages short. Then he says don't rush to change the code; check first whether the constraints are wrong. You spend the morning going through the constraint file. They are.
The institute canteen has twice-cooked pork at lunch. You take a plate and sit with the lab's young people, listening to them talk about who made Engineer this year and who's going on blind dates.

Joint debugging in the hardware lab. The board is hooked up to a signal generator and an oscilloscope; ADC data comes in and you capture waveforms in the ILA, twenty-odd times, until you finally see the sample point that won't line up.

Someone from the software lab asks why the FPGA's register map for the host computer doesn't match the document. You check: last month you changed an address and forgot to update the document. Red-faced, you fix it and send an email.

The program passes a milestone next month and the lab director has asked everyone to stay late this week. You eat a bowl of pea-and-minced-pork noodles at the little noodle shop downstairs, then go back to run place-and-route, forty minutes a pass.

The guard comes to lock the lab building. You take one last look at the timing report: zero violations. You take your phone out of the cabinet: a dozen-plus messages, one from your mother asking whether you're coming home this weekend.

ladder.title: Assistant Engineer
ladder.focus: Write RTL for modules, simulate and debug on the board under a mentor. You move up by closing timing on a subsystem and building the record for the mid-level title.

ladder.title: Engineer
ladder.focus: Own a subsystem's FPGA on your own, write your own constraints, take the project through milestones, and go to field trials.

ladder.title: Senior Engineer
ladder.focus: Own the whole signal processing subsystem, sign the design and test reports, train young engineers, and present the quality root-cause reviews.

ladder.title: Professor-level Senior Engineer
ladder.focus: Review proposals, audit program designs, choose components and architectures for new projects; one of the institute's technical final words.

ladder.title: Deputy Chief Designer
ladder.focus: Run the signal processing and digital parts of a major program, answerable for the technical design and every milestone review.

ai_tasks.name: Writing design documents, test reports and interface specs
ai_tasks.how: AI can draft design documents and test reports from the code, simulation results and templates, and compile IP interface descriptions. A person only needs to spot-check that the content matches the actual design.

ai_tasks.name: Writing RTL: state machines, FIFOs, common interfaces
ai_tasks.how: AI can write first-draft RTL from requirements. How the architecture and datapath are laid out, whether clock domains and resets are handled, and the high-speed and custom interfaces still need a person checking line by line.

ai_tasks.name: Writing testbenches, running simulations, guessing at bugs
ai_tasks.how: AI can write testbenches, generate stimulus and read simulation logs to suggest causes. But once on the board, hooking up the oscilloscope and seeing what the hardware actually does, a person has to be there to find the fault.

ai_tasks.name: Writing timing constraints and closing timing
ai_tasks.how: AI can explain timing reports and suggest constraints and optimizations. Closing timing means running the tools again and again and trading off against the device's characteristics; what to change, and whether it's worth it, is a person's call.

ai_tasks.name: Joint debugging with the hardware, software and systems teams
ai_tasks.how: Joint debugging takes the board and software working together on site, settling face to face whose problem it is, and the trade-offs and accountability before a milestone all rest on people. AI can only help look up documents and compile interface lists.

ai_tasks.name: Designing hardware acceleration for algorithms
ai_tasks.how: AI can help research algorithms, suggest ways to parallelize and roughly estimate resources and performance. Which architecture to choose, how to weigh latency, power and cost, and what the measured results show, a person decides.

events.e_timing: For three weeks you couldn't close timing on a high-speed interface. In the end you worked out for yourself how to split a large block of combinational logic into a three-stage pipeline, and for the first time closed it before your mentor stepped in. He read your code, didn't praise you, and signed the review form.
events.e_burnboard: During joint debugging you wired a power supply backwards, and a sample board worth tens of thousands of yuan gave off a puff of smoke. The veteran engineer from the hardware lab didn't shout. He took it apart with you, checked it component by component, replaced three chips, and the board lit up again.
events.e_zeroing: A unit failed at a customer site, and it was traced to a clock-domain crossing you wrote that was missing a synchronizer. The institute launched a formal quality root-cause review, and you wrote a dozen-page report, from symptom and cause to lessons for similar designs, and presented it page by page at the review meeting.
events.e_field: You went along on a field trial on the western Sichuan plateau, the ground station set up on a grassland at four thousand meters. At night your head ached too much to sleep, and you sat wrapped in an army greatcoat in the equipment shelter watching the antenna's satellite-tracking data. At dawn everything outside was frosted, and yaks were grazing in the distance.
events.e_node: The program passed a major milestone, the institute paid project bonuses, and the lab director took the whole lab out for hotpot. You drank two bottles of beer and for the first time felt that what was on that board was yours.
events.e_ai_rtl: The institute deployed a code model on its internal network that can write first-draft RTL for state machines, FIFOs and common interfaces from requirements, testbench included. You had it write a UART module and it passed simulation in ten minutes; you spent an afternoon tracking down the shortcut it took on reset.
events.e_ai_doc: AI can now draft design documents and test reports from the code and simulation results; a week's work for you now gets handed in within a day. Spot-checking, you found it had written a register's bit width wrong, and you added an automatic cross-check to the template.
events.e_domestic: The institute decided every new program would switch to Chinese-made FPGAs. Different toolchain, IP cores to redo. You spent a month feeling your way around the new development environment, filled half a notebook, and in the end moved the entire signal processing chain across.
events.e_award: The program you worked on won an industry science and technology progress award, and you were ninth on the list. The institute held a commendation ceremony in the big conference room. You went on stage to receive a certificate, and sent a photo of it to your parents.
events.e_phd: A PhD joined the lab and was appointed Engineer straight away, on noticeably more pay than you for much the same work. It stung a little. Later he came to you every day with questions about the boards, and you became the people who went for noodles together.
events.e_flat: You got a place in the institute's talent apartments: one bedroom and a living room, rent a third of the market rate, ten minutes' walk from the lab building. You grew two pots of chilies on the balcony, and in summer they gave a whole string.
events.e_house: You bought a flat in Pidu, half the down payment from the housing fund and your parents' savings. On handover day you stood in the empty flat working out the monthly mortgage: exactly a third of your pay plus the housing fund.
events.e_wedding: You got married. The banquet was at a farm restaurant back home, thirty tables set out in the open courtyard. Your lab colleagues hired a bus to come. Your mentor drank too much, took your hand and said: keep the board steady, and keep your life steady too.
events.e_child: Your child was born. For those months you tuned boards in the lab building by day, and at night walked the baby back and forth around the flat. Whenever the baby cried, you softly hummed a few register addresses.
events.e_checkup: The work health check said straightened cervical spine and fatty liver. You started playing half an hour of basketball on the institute court after work every day. After a month, a milestone broke the streak.
events.e_flatpay: At a class reunion, the ones who'd gone to private companies and to Shenzhen were all earning more than twice what you did. You said nothing over the hotpot. On the way home you added up the housing fund and the annuity, and decided it wasn't so bad.
events.e_parents: Your father went into hospital back home and you took leave. The hospital was only two hours from Chengdu, so you drove back and forth every day: the hospital by day, and at night back at the institute to hand over the board work.
events.e_master_retire: Your mentor retired. On the day he left he gave you a handwritten notebook of every pitfall he'd hit in twenty years. The last page said: constraints matter more than code.
events.e_apprentice: Your apprentice closed timing on a high-speed interface on his own for the first time and came running to tell you. You read his constraint file, signed the review form without praising him, and that evening bought him a bowl of noodles.
events.e_teahouse: One weekend you sat all afternoon in a teahouse in People's Park, fifteen yuan for a lidded cup of tea, old men beside you having their ears cleaned and playing mahjong. You thought about nothing, and never once took your phone out of your bag.
events.e_eyes: Years of staring at waveforms and timing reports left you farsighted, pushing your reading glasses up onto your forehead and pulling them down again to read the oscilloscope. The young ones laughed. You said: look at waveforms for twenty years and then talk.

c_master.title: Do a part-time engineering master's
c_master.situation: The institute runs a part-time master of engineering with a local university, half the tuition paid by the institute, classes at weekends. Finish it and your professional titles come a step sooner; but for three years every weekend is in a classroom, and when a milestone lands you'll have to ask for time off.

options.label: Do the degree
options.result: For three years you took the metro to class every weekend, and wrote your thesis on the FFT module in your own hands. At your defense, one of the panel was the institute's veteran chief designer.

options.label: Focus on the projects
options.result: You gave your weekends to the lab building and the boards, and that year wrote more code than anyone in the lab. Your mentor said you could already pull half a person's weight.

c_engineer.title: Apply for the mid-level title: Engineer
c_engineer.situation: You have enough years as an Assistant Engineer to apply for Engineer. You'll need a record of your work, two papers or patents, and to pass the institute's oral review. The lab has only two nominations this year, and four people are applying.

options.label: Apply
options.result: Your record of work described that timing you took three weeks to close, and how you reworked the pipeline. When the panel asked how you'd written the constraints, you drew a diagram on the whiteboard.

options.label: Give way to a colleague with more years
options.result: You said you'd apply next year. That year you wrote another patent, and the following year your file was twice as thick.

c_ai.title: Bring AI into your development process?
c_ai.situation: The code model is live on the institute's internal network, and the lab director asks who'll lead an effort to work out a process for using AI to write RTL and testbenches and generate documents, along with a set of review rules. It would take most of your spare time for half a year, and if it goes badly the old hands will laugh at you.

options.label: Lead the effort
options.result: Half a year later you'd produced a checklist, "Ten things to check in AI-written code": clock-domain crossings, resets, bit widths, nothing left out. Afterwards every new hire at the institute had to learn it first.

options.label: Get solid by hand first
options.result: You said you hadn't mastered the work yet and would leave it for now. That year you copied out your mentor's notebook from start to finish, adding your own notes after each entry.

c_private.title: A private telecoms company makes a big offer
c_private.situation: A private wireless equipment company in Tianfu Software Park is hiring FPGA engineers at one and a half times your current pay, with a year-end bonus tied to results. But there are no milestones or programs there; products iterate three times a year, overtime is routine, and there are no talent apartments or annuity.

options.label: Go private
options.result: In a year at the private company you shipped three products and learned to take an interface from nothing to mass production in two weeks. Your pay rose, your weekends shrank, and now and then you thought of the twice-cooked pork in the institute canteen.

options.label: Stay at the institute
options.result: You turned it down. That month the program passed its milestone, you drank two bottles of beer over hotpot, and thought this was fine too.

c_senior.title: Apply for the associate senior title: Senior Engineer
c_senior.situation: You can apply for Senior Engineer now: you'll need a record of leading a subsystem, papers and patents, and an oral defense before the provincial review committee. If you get it, you'll sign for the whole signal processing subsystem, train two or three young engineers, and sit in the front row at reviews.

options.label: Apply
options.result: At the defense you talked about that root-cause review, and said it taught you one thing: behind every line of code is a unit in a customer's hands. A veteran expert on the panel wrote on the scoring sheet for a long time.

options.label: Build up for two more years
options.result: You said your record wasn't substantial enough yet. In those two years you led the domestic-chip conversion of that chain, and the second time you applied, you didn't need to pad your file with anything.

c_chip.title: A chip company wants you for digital IC design
c_chip.situation: A communications chip company in Chengdu wants you for digital front-end design, saying your experience moving signal processing chains around on FPGAs is exactly what they lack. Double the pay, options on top; but it's another kind of work: what you write is etched into silicon and can't be changed.

options.label: Go into chips
options.result: You handed the phone cabinet key back to the guard. He said: come in and sit when you're passing.
options.end: From then on you did digital front-end design at the chip company. The modules you wrote went to tape-out and into many devices you never saw. You still write the constraints before the code; the young ones on the team call it a research-institute habit, and you say it's a good one.

options.label: Stay at the institute
options.result: You turned it down. That week you took your apprentice to a field trial, and on the grassland watched the antenna slowly lock onto the satellite.

c_college.title: A vocational college back home asks you to teach
c_college.situation: A vocational and technical college in your hometown of Mianyang has opened an electronic information program and wants you as a full-time teacher, guiding students through FPGA projects. About the same pay, winter and summer holidays, close to your parents; but you'll never again have something of yours installed in a ground station.

options.label: Go and teach
options.result: To your first class you brought a retired sample board, still carrying the label you wrote on it years ago. You had the students take turns capturing a signal with the oscilloscope.
options.end: You taught at the vocational college for many years, and your students went on to research institutes, factories and chip companies. Every year someone sends a screenshot of a timing report: teacher, zero violations.

options.label: Stay at the institute
options.result: You turned it down, but agreed to give two lectures a year at the college. The first time, you spent an afternoon on constraints.

options.label: Transfer internally to the quality office
options.result: You moved to the quality office, reviewing every lab's root-cause reports and design reviews. You became the person young engineers at the institute were most nervous of, and the one they most often came to ask on the quiet.

c_zhenggao.title: Apply for the full senior title: Professor-level Senior Engineer
c_zhenggao.situation: You can apply for Professor-level Senior Engineer now: you'll need to have led a complete program or major project, have awards and patents worth showing, and pass the provincial full-senior oral defense. If you get it, you're one of the few at the institute whose technical word is final, and at reviews the young ones will write down what you say.

options.label: Apply
options.result: At the defense you didn't talk about awards. You talked about the two hundred-odd pitfalls of those three years of domestic-chip conversion, and how you'd written them into an institute standard. The panel asked about your next step. You said: hand this standard to AI to check against, and have people decide whether its checks are right.

options.label: Don't apply; train your apprentices well
options.result: You said you'd rather spend a few more years in the lab building. Of the apprentices you trained, three later made Senior Engineer.

c_chief.title: Become a program's Deputy Chief Designer
c_chief.situation: The institute has launched a major new program and needs a Deputy Chief Designer over the signal processing and digital parts, answerable for the whole program's technical design and every milestone review. You'd negotiate specs with the customer, argue designs with the systems lab, and when something goes wrong, you're the first to stand up at the root-cause review.

options.label: Take it on
options.result: The first time you stood up at the program design review, the customer and dozens of experts sat below. When you finished, someone asked what worried you most. You said: that nobody's worried.

options.label: Recommend a younger engineer
options.result: You recommended your first apprentice and helped him with the design from behind the scenes. On the day he took the program through its first milestone, you sat in the back row of the meeting room.

endings.retire: On your last day you gave the handwritten notebook your mentor left you to the youngest person on the team, with your own notebook underneath it. You took your phone from the cabinet and handed the key to the guard. The guards had changed many times over, but this one still knew you. Outside the institute gate the ginkgoes of the western zone had turned yellow. You stood there a while, then took a shared bike home.
endings.burnout: That year two programs raced for milestones back to back, and you fainted once in the lab building. You went on sick leave and rested at home for most of a year, sitting every afternoon in the teahouse in People's Park, the lidded cup refilled again and again. One day an old man's radio crackled, and after listening a while you knew which band was bleeding in. You didn't say anything.

stages: Under your mentor you own one module's FPGA design: writing Verilog to the system design, simulating in ModelSim, running synthesis and place-and-route in Vivado, capturing waveforms in joint debugging at the hardware lab. You work most with your mentor and the hardware and software labs; your code only goes into the repository once your mentor signs the review form.

You own a subsystem's FPGA on your own: digital down-conversion, FFT and the high-speed interface to the ADC, the whole chain is yours. You write your own timing constraints, define your own interfaces, take the project through milestones and present your design at reviews. For field trials you're the one asked for by name, and an apprentice has started following you.

You own the whole signal processing subsystem and sign its design and test reports. You train two or three young engineers and review their code and constraints; in coordination meetings with the systems lab, the hardware lab and the customer's representative, you turn specs one by one into what's in the chip. When a quality problem arises, you present the root-cause report.

You're one of the few at the institute whose technical word is final: reviewing other labs' proposals, auditing program designs, choosing components and architectures for new projects. You write less code and sit through more reviews; when you say a design won't work, people stop to hear why. You still have a few apprentices.

You're deputy chief designer of a major program, over its signal processing and digital parts, answerable for the whole program's technical design and every milestone review. You negotiate specs with the customer, argue designs with the systems lab, and press institute leadership for people and money; at the root-cause review, you're first to stand. One habit remains: before a milestone, you go and look at the board.
work: A veteran engineer from the hardware lab handed you a new board and said the clock had a different crystal now. You regenerated the clock module, tested it on the board, and the jitter was half what it had been. He nodded.
Your mentor had you move a filter from its MATLAB model into the FPGA. You checked the fixed-point results bit by bit for two days until they finally lay on top of the curve in MATLAB.

A colleague in the software lab said the numbers the host read back were always off by one. You spent an afternoon capturing in the ILA and found the register read was one clock cycle short. When you'd fixed it he bought you a milk tea.

The new ADC doubled the sample rate, and the old interface couldn't keep up. You reconfigured the JESD204B link and stayed up all night in the lab building watching the bit-error-rate tester. Not a single error.

Your apprentice wrote a state machine that was perfect in simulation and locked up on the board. You had him pull up the reset waveform. He stared at it for ten minutes and found the register that never got reset himself.

During a field trial the ground station couldn't receive a signal, and the customer paced around the equipment shelter. You connected your laptop to the board, captured one waveform, found the local oscillator set to the wrong frequency, fixed it in ten minutes, and the signal came up.

The systems lab wanted a new function added to the subsystem, with ninety percent of resources already used. You and the young engineers shared the multipliers across three modules, freed up twenty percent, and the function went in.

A young engineer used AI to write some clock-domain-crossing code, and it passed simulation. In the review you had him explain why each synchronizer was placed where it was. At the third one, he stopped.

The customer's representative came to witness testing and pointed to a spec he said was 0.2 decibels short. You didn't argue. You laid out the test conditions and margins one by one, and in the end everyone signed the test report together.

A new project needed a component chosen: some argued for a bigger imported chip, others for a domestic one. You had both sides run the real signal chain, put resources, power and supply lead time in one table, and picked the domestic chip.

Another lab's root-cause report came to you for review, the cause beautifully written. You asked one question: how many other products at the institute use the same approach? They spent three days checking and found two more.

The institute wanted an FPGA design standard. You spread your mentor's notebook, your own and years of root-cause reports across the table, worked through them entry by entry, and wrote fifty pages. The last rule was still: constraints matter more than code.

At the program design review, the customer wanted one spec raised by another thirty percent. You worked through the night, and the next day brought three options, setting out exactly how much more each would cost and how much more risk it carried.

A week before a milestone, a subsystem prototype ran into trouble. You didn't have anyone stay up all night. You held an hour's meeting, split the problem into three lines of inquiry, and by the next morning each had an answer.

When the institute drew up a development plan for young engineers, you proposed one rule at the meeting: every new hire goes to at least one field trial in their first year, and watches an antenna lock onto a satellite from inside the shelter.
past: You went to middle school in Mianyang. Your father repaired equipment at an electronics factory, and the house was piled with old radios. You took one apart and couldn't put it back. He didn't scold you; he taught you to read the color bands on resistors.

In the gaokao (college entrance exam) you got into electronic information engineering at a university in Chengdu. You chose it because it was close to home, and at weekends you could take the bullet train back for dinner.

In your second year you entered the national electronic design contest and built a digital oscilloscope on an FPGA for the first time. The night before the contest the board failed, and you and your teammates stayed up in the lab until dawn. You won a provincial second prize.

In your third year you went to an open day at this institute and saw rows of racks and oscilloscopes in the lab building. A veteran engineer was tuning a board, and in a whole afternoon he never looked up.

In autumn recruiting in your final year you got an offer from a Shenzhen company at twice the pay, and one from this institute. You thought about it for a week in your dorm and chose the institute, because your parents said close to home was better.

In your year of probation your mentor had you write nothing at all, just read the FPGA code of one of the institute's old programs from start to finish. You read it for three months and drew hundreds of timing diagrams in your notebook.

late.pension_note: Estimate: the research institute pays pension contributions in full on actual salary and adds an occupational annuity, so the basic pension plus annuity comes to around sixty percent of your last monthly salary.
scenes: For the first week of retirement you still woke at seven-thirty every morning and reached for the phone cabinet key, touched your neck, and remembered you'd handed it in.
The institute rehired you to teach the design standard to young engineers. You didn't use slides. You drew a timing diagram on the whiteboard and had them find where it would go wrong.
Your grandchild took apart an old radio at home and couldn't put it back. You didn't scold him. You got out a magnifying glass and taught him to read the color bands on resistors.
In the first months of sick leave you slept until you woke on your own, then went for a stroll around the market downstairs and came back with a bunch of pea shoots.
You took to walking along the Jin River, from Jiuyan Bridge to Wangjiang Tower, and when you were tired you sat at a riverside tea stall watching people fly kites.

An old colleague came over for tea and said the new program had passed another milestone, then brought up that timing you took three weeks to close all those years ago. You laughed and refilled his cup.
In your first year on a different path, every time you passed the western high-tech zone you glanced toward the institute to see how many lights were still on in the lab building.
On an errand back at the institute, the guard at the gate was someone new. You gave your name, and the person who came out to meet you was the apprentice you'd once trained.
On the news you saw a report of a ground station opening, the footage flashing by. You recognized the racks in the equipment shelter at a glance. They were your institute's.
Back home in Mianyang, your father had long since stopped repairing equipment, but the pile of old radios was still under the bed. You took one out, replaced a capacitor, and it played again.
In a cupboard you found the digital oscilloscope board from your second year, its solder joints crooked. You powered it up, and a sine wave actually came up on the screen.

closing.retire: One afternoon many years later you sat in the teahouse in People's Park as the lidded cup was refilled for the third time. The old man's radio beside you crackled, then came clear. You listened to the Sichuan opera on it, and didn't wonder which band it was coming in on.
closing.burnout: Many years later you sat on a bench by the Jin River. An egret stood on the water, and ripples spread out ring after ring. You watched them, one ring after another, and didn't count their period.
closing.end: Many years later you found an old key to the institute's phone cabinet in a drawer; somehow you'd never handed it back. You looked at it in your palm a while, then put it back.
